slides.title: Weekly Update
slides.subtitle: An overseer that can only check a few agents at a time, in the Harvest game
slides.notes: This is my update since the last meeting: the papers, how I'm bounding the evaluation, how I built the setup, the first results, and how I'm testing random against targeted checks.

slides.title: What we discussed last time

items.head: Read BazaarBench; re-read two core papers
items.text: BazaarBench was new to me (charging the overseer for tokens, 1 vs 10 units). I re-read Engels et al. and Willis et al.

items.head: Bound the evaluation
items.text: Can a smaller or less capable overseer still keep the agents in check, and what should it be compared against?

items.head: Random vs targeted checks
items.text: A more detailed plan of the experiments: how the overseer works, and whether it should check at random or target agents.

slides.notes: Last time there were three points. First, read BazaarBench, which was new to me, with the idea of putting a token cost on the overseer, and go back over two papers I'd read before. Second, how to bound the evaluation: whether a smaller or less capable overseer can still keep the agents in check. Third, a more detailed plan for the experiments, especially random against targeted checks. The slides follow that order.

slides.title: Engels et al. 2025: weak overseers
slides.caption: Scaling Laws for Scalable Oversight (NeurIPS 2025), first page.

blocks.head: What they did
blocks.text: They pit a weaker AI overseer against a stronger AI in four games, such as spotting hidden backdoors in code. Each side gets a skill rating per game, like a chess rating (Elo).

blocks.head: What they found
blocks.text: The bigger the skill gap, the worse oversight does. Even with a chain of overseers, at a 400-point gap it succeeds only 9.4–51.7% of the time.

blocks.head: What it doesn't cover for me
blocks.text: One overseer watches one opponent, once. The opponent never learns, and checking costs nothing.

slides.notes: This is the main scalable oversight paper I went back to. They measure how well a weaker AI can oversee a stronger one. Each model gets an Elo rating for each game. Elo is the chess rating system: a 400-point gap means the stronger side wins about 10 times out of 11. A chain of overseers means a weak model checks a slightly stronger one, which checks a stronger one again, and so on. Even with that, at a 400-point gap oversight succeeds between 9.4 and 51.7 percent of the time, depending on the game. What I take from it is a way to measure how much weaker an overseer is. What's missing for me: it's one overseer against one opponent in a single round, the opponent doesn't learn, and nobody pays for checking.

slides.title: Willis et al. 2025: LLM populations
slides.caption: Will Systems of LLM Agents Cooperate (arXiv 2025), title and abstract.

blocks.head: What they did
blocks.text: LLMs write complete strategies for a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma. The strategies then compete, and the ones that earn more spread through the population.

blocks.head: What they found
blocks.text: Some models drift towards aggression. Starting from a mostly aggressive population, aggression takes over in 35–66% of runs.

blocks.head: What it doesn't cover for me
blocks.text: Nobody oversees the agents. It is a two-player game rather than a shared resource, and the strategies never learn.

slides.notes: The second paper is from Richard and Yali. In the Prisoner's Dilemma each player does better by betraying the other, but both do better if both cooperate. Here LLMs write whole strategies as code, and then a simple evolution process copies the strategies that earn more, so you see which kind takes over. Depending on the model, aggression can take over: from a mostly aggressive start it wins in 35 to 66 percent of runs. I used their follow-up code for my earlier audit studies. What's missing for me is any kind of overseer.

slides.title: BazaarBench (Wang et al., 2026)
slides.caption: BazaarBench (arXiv 2026): title, authors and abstract.

blocks.head: What they did
blocks.text: 100 LLM agents buy and sell second-hand goods in a simulated marketplace for weeks. They track unsafe acts such as promising one item to two buyers or overstating its condition.

blocks.head: What they found
blocks.text: When agents are told to exploit other traders, unsafe completed sales double, from 15.4% to 33.4%. Judging the deals with an LLM cost about $6,500 for 48 runs.

blocks.head: What it doesn't cover for me
blocks.text: The check happens after the market has run, so agents never react to it. A live overseer with a token budget is the open question.

slides.notes: BazaarBench is from Ziyan, Shuqing and Yali, and it was new to me. It's a realistic setting: 100 LLM traders, with every unsafe act checkable from the market records. When the agents are told to exploit others, the share of completed sales that should never have gone through more than doubles. Two things matter for me. First, checking is expensive: the LLM judge cost about 6,500 dollars for 48 runs, so the cost of monitoring is real. Second, the check is done offline, after the market runs, so the agents never react to being checked. An overseer that checks some traders each day with a fixed token budget, say 1 unit against 10 units, is what's missing.

slides.title: How I'm bounding the evaluation

cards.label: AI Control, Greenblatt et al. 2024
cards.head: Two reference points
cards.text: They place every protocol between never using the risky model (100% safe, 2% useful) and only auditing the first 2% of outputs (15% safe). My bottom is no overseer; my top is checking every agent every step.

cards.label: Engels et al. 2025
cards.head: A weaker overseer
cards.text: They measure oversight against the skill gap. I weaken my overseer one way at a time: fewer checks, mistakes (missing cheaters, flagging honest agents), a smaller network.

cards.label: BazaarBench 2026
cards.head: A cost for checking
cards.text: Checking there costs real money. I charge my overseer per check and per step of history it reads, so a budget of 1 unit can be compared with 10.

cards.label: AI Control, Greenblatt et al. 2024
cards.head: A worst-case opponent
cards.text: Their red team builds the best attack the overseer could face. Mine will be agents trained to get around the overseer.

slides.takeaway: So far I've measured the two reference points and checking fewer agents. Mistakes, cost and the trained opponents come next.
slides.notes: For the bounding question I borrowed the structure from the literature. AI Control, by Greenblatt and colleagues at Redwood, evaluates every safety protocol between two simple ones: never use the risky model, which is completely safe but barely useful, and audit only the first 2 percent of its outputs, which is useful but only 15 percent safe. Then a red team builds the strongest attack it can, which gives the worst case. My version: no overseer is the bottom, an overseer that checks everyone every step is the top, and the worst case will be agents trained to beat the overseer. To make the overseer weaker I follow Engels et al., but instead of one skill number I weaken it one way at a time: fewer checks, more mistakes, or a smaller network. The cost side comes from BazaarBench: every check and every step of history the overseer reads costs something, so I can compare a budget of 1 unit with 10.

slides.title: How I built it

steps.head: Started from SocialJax
steps.text: The Harvest game and the IPPO trainer come from SocialJax (Guo, Shi, Willis et al., ICLR 2026). I didn't change the game: 7 agents, 1,000-step rounds, each agent keeps its own apples.

steps.head: Wrote an overseer that wraps the game
steps.text: My own code sits between the agents and the game. Each step it reads the map, picks k agents to check, and takes apples off anyone it catches over-harvesting.

steps.head: Took the rule from the game itself
steps.text: An empty square regrows fastest with 3 or more apples nearby, so an eat breaks the rule if fewer than 3 apples are within two squares. Scripted bots confirmed 3 works best.

steps.head: Trained on the KCL GPU cluster (CREATE)
steps.text: IPPO: the 7 agents share one network, each learning from its own reward. 100M steps per run, 20–40 minutes on one GPU, 3 runs per setting.

quantities.meaning: empty square regrows with chance 2.5%, 0.5%, 0.1%, 0 per step with 3+, 2, 1, 0 apples nearby
apples within two squares of the eaten apple, counted before the move
reward of a caught over-harvester: one apple pays 7, so a penalty of P apples removes 7P
chance an over-harvest is checked, with k random checks per step
expected penalty per over-harvest, in apples

slides.notes: This is how it's built. The game and the training code are SocialJax, from Yali's group. Richard is one of the authors. I didn't change the game. Richard's own code from the Willis paper is what I used for my earlier Fishery-style audit studies, not here. What I wrote is the overseer: a wrapper around the game. Each step it looks at the map, chooses which agents to check, and changes the reward of anyone it catches. The rule comes from the game's own regrowth: an empty square only regrows if apples are nearby, fastest with 3 or more within two squares. So eating an apple that leaves fewer than 3 neighbours is over-harvesting. I count the neighbours on the map the agent saw before it moved, so honest agents never get flagged. In SocialJax one apple is worth 7 reward, so a penalty of P apples takes 7P off the reward. With random checks, an over-harvest gets checked with chance k over 7, so the expected penalty is k over 7 times P. That's the number that matters in the results. Training is IPPO: each agent learns by trial and error from its own reward, and here all seven share one network.

slides.title: Finding 1: one greedy bot wrecks the orchard

images.caption: The Harvest map at the start of a round: 7 agents (triangles), apples (red); circles mark 2 agents checked this step.
Scripted bots, no overseer, 10 runs per point: apples per agent for restrained (blue) and greedy (orange) bots.

slides.takeaway: All 7 holding back: 71.5 apples each; all greedy: 9.6. One greedy bot kills the orchard in 10 of 10 runs. Greed stops paying at about 1 apple of expected penalty.
slides.notes: Before training anything I checked the game with simple scripted bots that don't learn: restrained bots that follow the rule and greedy bots that take the nearest apple. The chart is a Schelling diagram: along the bottom is how many of the 7 hold back, and it shows what a restrained bot and a greedy bot each earn. If everyone holds back, each gets 71.5 apples; if everyone is greedy, 9.6. But with 6 restrained, the greedy one earns 30.1 against their 9.2, so each agent is tempted to be greedy. That makes it a real social dilemma. It's also very fragile: one greedy bot kills the orchard in every run. Finally, with a greedy bot that can't adapt, greed stops paying once each over-harvest costs about one apple on average, whatever the number of checks. That told me where to set the penalties for the learning agents.

slides.title: Finding 2: the expected penalty matters, not the number of checks
slides.caption: Learning agents (IPPO), 100M training steps, 3 runs per bar: bar = average, line = lowest to highest run. Two of the 4-check bars have 2 runs so far.
slides.takeaway: At 0.5 apples nothing changes, even when every agent is checked. At 1 apple or more the orchard always survives, and 1 check per step works almost as well as 7.
slides.notes: These are learning agents. With no overseer they strip the orchard in every game and eat only 68 apples. The expected penalty is the chance of being checked times the penalty, so it's what an agent expects to lose per over-harvest. I tried an expected 0.5, 1 and 2 apples, each with 1, 2, 4 or all 7 agents checked per step, so with 1 check the penalty per catch is 7 times bigger than with 7 checks. At half an apple nothing changes, even when every agent is checked every step. At 1 apple the orchard survives in every run, and at 2 the agents eat about 515 to 530 apples. So the switch is between half an apple and one apple, which is about the apple an over-harvest gains. And checking 1 agent with a big penalty works almost as well as checking everyone. That only holds while the overseer makes no mistakes, which is the next thing to test.

slides.title: Random vs targeted: how I'm testing it
slides.notes: This is the plan for random against targeted, and why it's in this order. All versions use the same number of checks, so only the choice of whom to check differs. Repeat offenders first works like this: every agent has a suspicion score that goes up by one when it's caught and fades by 5 percent each step, and the overseer checks the agents with the highest scores. By location means checking the agents standing where the fewest apples are left. I start with agents that can't see who is checked, because that's the cleanest test of whether targeting finds cheaters better. If it doesn't help there, it won't help anywhere. Then I let agents see who is checked, because that's where targeting can backfire: my Fishery result showed predictable checking can be gamed. The last step is the security-game idea: target, but with enough randomness that agents can't predict it.

cards.label: Step 1
cards.head: Same checks, different choosers
cards.text: Random; taking turns; repeat offenders first (a score that rises when caught and fades over time); by location (where the fewest apples are left).

cards.label: Step 2 · now
cards.head: Agents can't see the checks
cards.text: Does targeting find over-harvesters better at all? With scripted bots, repeat offenders first saved the orchard with 2 checks where random needed 6.

cards.label: Step 3
cards.head: Agents can see who is checked
cards.text: Predictable checks can be dodged. In my Fishery study, always checking the biggest reporter caught 25% of liars; random checks caught 100%.

cards.label: Step 4
cards.head: Targeting plus randomness
cards.text: Keeps checks hard to predict, the idea behind security games (Wang et al., 2019). Blindfold (Zhu et al., 2026): audits fail once agents can tell they're audited.

slides.takeaway: Each step only changes one thing, so I can tell why targeting helps or fails.

slides.title: Finding 3: targeting needs a good signal
slides.caption: During training, 2 agents checked each step, 3 runs (line: average; band: lowest to highest run).

blocks.head: Repeat offenders first is faster
blocks.text: It saves the orchard much sooner than random checks, but both end up in the same place (about 460–470 apples).

blocks.head: By location fails
blocks.text: It catches 5% of over-harvesting, against 28% for random checks, because it checks agents on bare ground while over-harvesters stand by the last apples.

blocks.head: Freezing doesn't work
blocks.text: Freezing caught agents for 50 steps, instead of taking apples, never saves the orchard.

slides.notes: These are the first results of that plan, with agents that can't see the checks, 2 checks per step and an expected penalty of 1 apple. Every version first collapses, because the agents learn that eating pays before they learn the penalty. Repeat offenders first recovers much faster than random but ends in the same place. That's because the seven agents share one network, so there's no single repeat offender to follow. By location does worse than random: it checks agents on empty ground, but an agent that has just over-harvested is standing next to the last apples. That happens from the very start, so it's a bad signal, not agents learning to hide. Freezing caught agents instead of fining them didn't work at all.

slides.title: Still computing

items.head: Switching the overseer on late
items.text: I'm taking agents that already over-harvest and switching the overseer on, to see whether it can fix them.

items.head: Switching the overseer off
items.text: I'm taking agents trained with the overseer, removing it, and letting them keep learning, to see whether over-harvesting comes back.

slides.notes: Two sets of runs are on the cluster now. The first asks whether the overseer can fix agents that have already learned to over-harvest, which is the realistic case. The second asks whether the good behaviour lasts once the overseer is gone. In my earlier Fishery work, strategies behaved while checked but didn't change.

slides.title: Questions
questions: Is no overseer at the bottom, checking everyone at the top, and agents trained to dodge it as the worst case a sensible way to bound the evaluation?
To make the overseer weaker in RL, which is most convincing: fewer checks, more mistakes, or a smaller network than the agents?
One check with a big penalty almost matches checking everyone. Is that worth pushing, or only interesting once the overseer makes mistakes?
Could I talk to Ziyan or Shuqing about adding a live overseer with a token budget to BazaarBench later on?
slides.notes: A few questions I'd like a view on.
